questions.prompt: In the example, the four fit windows averaged a Sharpe ratio of 1.10 and the joined test years scored 0.38. Which number estimates how the rule would have traded?
options: 1.10, because it uses twice as much data
0.38, because every test year was unseen by the fit that chose the length
questions.explanation: Each fit score is the best of 5 on the data that chose it, so it carries luck. The test years played no part in any choice, so their joined score of 0.38 is the honest one.

questions.prompt: With a 2-year rolling fit window, which years are used to choose the length for the 2022 test?
questions.explanation: A rolling window keeps a fixed length and moves forward. For a 2022 test, the 2 years before it are 2020 and 2021.

questions.prompt: Why is a single out-of-sample split a weaker test than walk-forward for a rule that is refitted each year?
options: A single split cannot compute a Sharpe ratio
Walk-forward uses the test data to choose the length
A single split gives one verdict on one fixed fit, while walk-forward tests each refit the way it would run
questions.explanation: Walk-forward repeats fit, test and roll, so it tests the refitting itself and gives four test years instead of one stretch. The test data still never chooses anything.
